subject: knight
pitch: A fantasy knight in battle-worn plate armour. A great helm with a narrow eye slit and a tall crimson plume, layered shoulder plates etched with gold filigree, a deep-blue surcoat with a silver griffin emblem, a tall kite shield bearing the same griffin, and a broadsword. Dents and scratches tell of many battles, and a torn crimson cape hangs from the shoulders.
reasoning:
I'm uncertain about the exact API signatures, so I need to work carefully from what I can infer—likely something like b.joint taking name, position, and orientation parameters, and b.part needing similar structural arguments plus geometry and color that I'm not fully sure of.

I'll default to relying on nearest-bone assignment for parts rather than specifying explicit bones, and use directional parameters sparingly for rotation—keeping arms hanging straight and the sword blade vertical to minimize risk, while allowing a bit more tilt for something like a cape.

Now I'm sketching out the skeleton structure: hips as root joint, then spine up through chest, neck, head, and jaw, plus shoulder/elbow/wrist chains for each arm and hip/knee/ankle chains for each leg, sized for a roughly 1.85m knight with feet at floor level. I'm planning helper functions for boxes, cylinders, and spheres, and picking out a palette of steel, gold, crimson, silver, and leather tones, then figuring out how to approximate a griffin emblem on the surcoat using simple geometric primitives since I don't have a decal or SVG function available.

I'm working out the helmet plume as stacked crimson shapes, the helmet itself as a boxy cylinder with a dark eye slit and separate jaw joint, then moving on to positioning the sword vertically in the right hand at a manageable length and shaping the shield as a tapered kite form using stacked boxes on the left arm.

For the shield construction I'm planning tapering widths rather than true extrusion, then shifting to writing a general limb helper function that builds cylinder segments between two joint points, computing direction and midpoint automatically so arms and legs can be posed with a slight A-pose tilt.

Now I'm placing joint coordinates for shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, and ankles to define the arm and leg poses, then designing a tattered cape as a series of varied-length strips hanging behind the shoulders, tilted backward slightly, built using the same segment helper between top and bottom points. Writing geometry code...
